passage: It started on a Tuesday last month. I said "Good morning" to Ishita and she looked straight past me, like I was a window. At lunch, the four of them sat at the other end of the bench and talked in low voices. Nobody said anything mean. Nobody said anything at all. That was the worst part. If they'd teased me, at least I'd know what I did. I kept going over everything: the pencil I didn't return? The game I won? My stomach felt like it had a stone in it all day. That night Amma asked why I wasn't eating. I cried and told her. She sat with me and said, "Aditi, this isn't your fault. Tomorrow I'll talk to your class teacher." She did. It still took a week to feel normal again.

qa.q: What did Aditi say to Ishita on that Tuesday?
qa.a: Aditi said "Good morning", and Ishita looked straight past, like at a window.

qa.q: Why does Aditi say the silence was worse than teasing?
qa.a: With no words at all there was no clue about what went wrong, so Aditi felt confused and anxious, searching for a reason.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what made Amma's response helpful?
qa.a: The turning point was telling Amma; she listened, said it wasn't Aditi's fault, and spoke to the class teacher the next day.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel if she saw how much Aditi was hurting?
qa.a: Ishita might feel surprised or guilty, since ignoring someone can seem harmless to the person doing it.

grounding: A child whose friends suddenly stop speaking to them feels invisible, anxious and confused, finding the silence worse than teasing.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5C, Friday
For three days Nandini has been sitting alone during group work. Sunaina and the girls she usually sits with move their chairs when she comes near and talk to each other, never to her. No names, no teasing, just silence. Nandini asked me twice to go to the washroom during maths and came back with red eyes. Today she said, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke. It wasn't.
What I did: I sat with Nandini at break and listened. She has no idea what she did. I told her it was not her fault and that I would help. I spoke with Sunaina separately; she said the group was "upset about the sleepover". I have called both families this evening, and on Monday the counsellor and I will sit with the girls together.

qa.q: What did Nandini ask the teacher today?
qa.a: Nandini asked, "Ma'am, am I invisible?" and laughed as if it were a joke.

qa.q: What do Nandini's red eyes and joking question suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: They suggest she feels hurt, anxious and confused, and is trying to hide how much the silence affects her.

qa.q: Which of the teacher's steps matter most, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Nandini and saying it isn't her fault calms her right away, and talking to Sunaina and the families opens a way to find out what went wrong.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the silence, given the comment about the sleepover?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel the group had a real grievance, without realising that silence hurts Nandini more than saying what upset them.

grounding: A teacher records a child frozen out by her friends, who feels invisible and confused, and takes steps the same day.

passage:
Wednesday
Day two of nobody talking to me. Ayesha passed the chalk box down the row and skipped me. Skipped me! Like my desk was empty. When I asked her about the science chart, she turned and asked Deepa what time it was. I didn't know that could hurt so much. I kept checking my bag for something I might have done wrong. Was it the birthday card? Did I talk too much at the picnic? I don't know, and not knowing makes my stomach flip over and over.
At dinner Paati asked why I was stirring my rasam and not drinking it. I told her everything. She didn't say "ignore them". She held my hand and said we'll tell Miss tomorrow, together, and that I haven't done anything to deserve silence.
I feel a bit lighter. Not much. A bit.
Kavitha

qa.q: What did Ayesha pass down the row?
qa.a: Ayesha passed the chalk box down the row and skipped Kavitha.

qa.q: What worry is making Kavitha's stomach flip over and over?
qa.a: Not knowing what went wrong; Kavitha keeps searching for a mistake, and the not-knowing fills Kavitha with worry.

qa.q: What choice at dinner changed how Kavitha felt?
qa.a: Kavitha chose to tell Paati everything, and Paati's hand, her plan to tell Miss together, and her reassurance made Kavitha feel a bit lighter.

qa.q: How might Paati feel hearing about the chalk box and the silence?
qa.a: Paati probably feels protective and sad, which is why she doesn't brush it off and plans to act the next day.

grounding: A child ignored by friends in class feels invisible and anxious about what they did wrong, and a grandmother responds with care.

passage: In the village school near Dharwad, Vidya, ten, walked in on Monday and said, "Hi," to her three friends. They looked at their slates. At lunch under the tamarind tree they sat in a tight circle, backs to her. Nobody said anything mean. Nobody said anything at all. By Wednesday Vidya was checking her memory for what she had done. The ribbon she forgot to return? Winning at kho-kho? Her stomach felt heavy all day. She almost wished they would shout. That evening her brother Jeevan noticed her rice going cold. "What's wrong?" Vidya burst into tears. Amma came and sat with her, listened to all of it and said, "You haven't done anything to deserve this." Then she walked with Vidya to the teacher's house that same evening to tell her.

qa.q: Where did Vidya's friends sit at lunch?
qa.a: They sat in a tight circle under the tamarind tree, with their backs to her.

qa.q: Why did Vidya almost wish her friends would shout?
qa.a: Being ignored left her confused and anxious about what she had done, and a shout would at least have told her something.

qa.q: What choice by Amma helped most, and why?
qa.a: Amma listened, told Vidya she had not deserved it and took her to the teacher that same evening, so she was not left alone with the silence.

qa.q: How did Jeevan notice something was wrong?
qa.a: He saw his sister's rice going cold, which told him she was upset even before she spoke.

grounding: A ten-year-old whose friends stop speaking to her feels invisible, anxious and confused, and her mother acts the same day.

passage: On Tuesday Abebe, eleven, said, "Hey," to Mei and the others at his table in their Melbourne classroom. Mei turned to talk to Liam as if Abebe were not there. At recess the group walked away. In science, when Abebe asked Mei to pass the ruler, she passed it to Liam instead, who dropped it by Abebe without looking. No one had teased him. Ms Walsh, the librarian, found him, sat on the floor beside him and listened. "This is not your fault," she said, and before the final bell she had spoken to his teacher and phoned his dad.

passage: When I was eleven, my three best friends, including Naveen, suddenly stopped talking to me. No fight, no reason. One Monday I said "hi" and they looked through me like I was a window. At lunch they moved tables. When I asked Naveen what I'd done, he walked away. I felt invisible. I kept thinking back over everything: was it my birthday party? something I'd said? I'd rather they'd shouted at me. At least then I'd know. That evening I finally told Mummy, crying into the dal. She put her spoon down, held me, and said, "You haven't done anything to deserve this." She called my class teacher that night. The next day Ma'am sat us all down together. It didn't fix everything. But I stopped feeling like a ghost. I'm Jasleen, and I still remember that week.

qa.q: How many best friends stopped talking to Jasleen?
qa.a: Jasleen's three best friends stopped talking.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when the friends looked through Jasleen like a window?
qa.a: Jasleen felt invisible, anxious and confused, not knowing what had gone wrong.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She listened, said Jasleen hadn't deserved it, and called the teacher that same night, so an adult could step in the next day.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt walking away when asked?
qa.a: Naveen might have felt awkward or guilty, not able to explain the silence to a friend.

grounding: A child whose friends suddenly give the silent treatment feels invisible, anxious and confused, until an adult responds the same day.

passage:

For three days, Kishore (class five) has been ignored by his group of friends. Baljeet seems to have started it. They don't answer when he speaks, they turn their chairs away, and at lunch they scatter when he sits down. Kishore looks tired and has stopped raising his hand. This afternoon I spoke with Baljeet and the group separately; it seems to be about a cricket match. I've called Kishore's parents this evening, and on Monday I'll seat Kishore with a kind new classmate for group work.

passage:
Thursday
Kashish and Mona and Aisha didn't talk to me AGAIN today. I said good morning. Nothing. In PT, I stood next to them and they just walked to the other side. It's like I'm air.
I don't even know what I did. I keep thinking and thinking. Maybe it was when I didn't lend Kashish my gel pen? Maybe I'm boring.
I wish they would just be mean. Then at least they'd be looking at me.
I told Mummy after dinner. She sat on my bed and listened to everything. She said it's not my fault and that feeling invisible is one of the worst feelings. She's going to talk to Ma'am tomorrow morning before school, and she'll walk me in. She's letting me sleep with the light on tonight.
- Nandini

passage:
In the village school, Dhruv's two best friends had always saved him a spot under the neem tree. On Monday, Leela and the other boy walked past him as if he wasn't there.
"Leela?" he called. She looked away.

On Thursday, he told his Ma he had a headache and didn't want to go to school.
His Ma looked at him for a long time and asked, "Did something happen with your friends?"

passage:
In Seoul, Soo-ah had walked to school with Chen every day for two years. Then one Monday, Chen didn't wait at the corner.
In class, when Soo-ah passed him a note, he slid it back without reading it. Two other girls who usually sat with Soo-ah moved their desks slightly away.
Nobody said anything mean. That was the strange part. It was as if Soo-ah had turned into air.
At home, she lay on her bed and made a list: Was it my birthday party? My joke about his haircut? Something I didn't even notice?
"It would be easier if they just yelled at me," she told her older sister.
Her sister sat beside her. "Tomorrow, let's talk to your teacher together."

passage:
In the school library, Harsha sat at the usual table and opened a book. Samir and the others were at the next table. Last week they had all been together.
Harsha said, "Did you finish the science worksheet?"
Nobody answered. Samir turned a page. Someone coughed.
Harsha's face went hot. For the rest of the period, Harsha didn't read a word. What had happened? Was it the cricket match? The lunch swap?
The librarian noticed Harsha staring at the same page. At the bell, the librarian stopped Harsha at the door. "You look worried. Want to talk to your class teacher? I can walk you there."
Harsha nodded slowly.

passage: Sit, Yash. You're sulking because your friends went quiet on you? Let me tell you about the Onam when I was a girl of ten. My three best friends and I made the pookalam together every year. That year, on the first morning, they just didn't call for me. At school they whispered and stopped when I came near. Nobody said a word to me. Not a single cruel word, either. That was the worst part. If they'd teased me, at least I'd know what I'd done. I stopped eating properly. Finally my amma walked me to the eldest girl's house and asked her mother to let us talk. It was over a torn ribbon I didn't even remember. Your Rukmini Ammamma cried that night, Yash, with relief.

passage: The bus to the winter picnic was full, and the fog meant it crawled. Gurpreet had saved a seat for Aman, but Aman sat with the others at the back. For two hours, with no room to move and no signal on his phone, Gurpreet stared at the seat in front. He wondered what he'd done. Was it the cricket match? His stomach tightened. At the stop, Nitin from the other section sat beside him with a packet of peanuts. "Want some?" Gurpreet nodded, afraid his voice would crack. Later he told Nitin, who walked with him straight to their class teacher that afternoon.

At lunch she ate her paratha very slowly. That evening Mummy found her on the stairs, still in uniform. "They're not angry," Parul whispered. "They're just not seeing me."
